analysis.one_liner: Tears down the legal walls separating banks, securities firms, and insurance companies into single conglomerates.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 214-213, and the Senate voted 93-0 and then 88-11 just to open debate, but the Senate adjourned for the year without ever voting on the bill itself, and it died.
analysis.plain_summary: Since the 1930s, laws like the Glass-Steagall Act kept banks, securities firms, and insurance companies separate, so a bank could not underwrite stocks or an insurer could not own a bank. This bill would repeal those walls and let large financial companies combine into one conglomerate offering banking, investments, and insurance together. It also makes it easier for bank mergers to win antitrust approval, limits the Federal Reserve's ability to examine the new nonbank affiliates, and adds some consumer protections, like requiring banks to offer low-cost basic accounts as a condition of expanding.
analysis.who_benefits: Large bank holding companies, securities firms, and insurance companies, which would be allowed to merge into financial conglomerates and cross-sell each other's products. Smaller banks would get some Federal Home Loan Bank lending flexibilities, and consumers would gain guaranteed low-cost basic bank accounts and a complaint process for bank-sold investment products — but these are conditions attached to a large deregulation of the biggest institutions.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Big banks, securities firms, and insurers

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the Glass-Steagall provisions that bar a Federal Reserve member bank from affiliating with a securities firm, and repeals the ban on officers or directors serving at both a bank and a securities firm.

Creates financial holding companies that, if their banks are well capitalized and well managed, can engage in lending, insurance, securities underwriting, and investment advisory activities without prior case-by-case approval for many activities.
Requires financial holding companies to offer low-cost basic banking accounts and hold a satisfactory Community Reinvestment Act rating as a condition of expanded powers.
Requires federal banking agencies to write consumer protection rules and set up a complaint process for investment and insurance products sold by banks, including rules on coercion and disclosure.
Modernizes the Federal Home Loan Bank system, including expanding the Affordable Housing Program to direct subsidies on advances for low- and moderate-income housing.
Creates the National Association of Registered Agents and Brokers to provide uniform multistate licensing for insurance agents, preserving state authority over consumer protection.
Adds a Financial Information Privacy Act title making it a federal violation to obtain bank customers' financial information under false pretenses, with civil and criminal penalties.

analysis.who_pays: Depositors and taxpayers, through the federal deposit insurance funds, bear the risk if a conglomerate's securities or insurance affiliate runs into trouble and the trouble spreads to the insured bank — the bill responds by limiting, not expanding, the Federal Reserve's ability to examine those affiliates. Consumers of bank-sold investment products lose the legal clarity that their products are not FDIC-insured, which the bill addresses only with a study. Communities face faster bank consolidation because the bill removes the regulatory bar against approving mergers that create monopolies and strips competitive-factor review from the approval process.
analysis.who_pays_short: Depositors, taxpayers, and communities facing consolidation

drawbacks.text: Repeals the prohibition on regulatory approval of bank mergers that would create a monopoly and removes competitive-effects review from the regulators' approval process, leaving antitrust screening mainly to the Attorney General.

Bars the Federal Reserve from taking most supervisory or enforcement action against a new nonbank affiliate — a broker-dealer, insurer, or investment adviser — unless it poses a material risk to an affiliated insured bank or the payment system.

Lets banks newly acquired by a holding company be excluded from Community Reinvestment Act community-credit requirements for roughly two years after acquisition while an improvement plan is approved and completed.
Investment and insurance products sold through banks are not FDIC-insured, but the bill responds to that confusion only by directing a study of how to inform customers, not by requiring disclosure.

The privacy title covers only obtaining customer information under false pretenses; it does not restrict how a combined banking-securities-insurance company shares its own customers' information among affiliates.

The bill orders a GAO study of its impact on financial institutions with $100 million or less in assets, an acknowledgment that consolidation of the largest firms could squeeze smaller community banks.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer provisions — low-cost accounts, complaint processes, disclosure rules, privacy enforcement — are real but modest and are structured as conditions for letting the largest financial firms combine. The core of the bill is a large expansion of what those firms may do, paired with a weaker antitrust screen for bank mergers and reduced Federal Reserve oversight of new affiliates. The promised consumer benefits depend on regulators using the remaining tools well, while the risks — concentration of financial power and contagion from nonbank affiliates into insured banks — are borne by depositors and the deposit insurance funds.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it by a single vote in May 1998; the Senate Banking Committee reported its own version and senators voted 88-11 just to open debate in October, but the Senate never reached a vote on passage before the Congress ended, and the bill died.

narrative.text: The bill spent over a year in two House committees, which reported it in amended form in July and November 1997, before the House passed it by a recorded vote of 214-213 on May 13, 1998.
The House vote split heavily by party: 153 of 227 Republicans voted yes while 139 of 205 Democrats voted no, leaving the bill's passage dependent on a single vote.
The Senate Banking Committee, chaired by Senator D'Amato, held four days of hearings in June 1998 and reported the bill with its own substitute amendment on September 18, 1998.
On October 5, 1998, the Senate voted 93-0 to cut off debate on a motion to proceed, and on October 7 it agreed to the motion to proceed 88-11, with only 6 Republicans and 5 Democrats voting no.

The Senate considered the bill on October 8-9, 1998, and the last action in the record is Senator Lott's motion to recommit the bill to committee and his proposed amendments on October 9; no vote on passage ever occurred.
The 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999, with the bill having passed the House but never having come to a final vote in the Senate.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The large financial firms that pushed the bill lost only time: Congress enacted substantially similar legislation the following year, and the combining of banks, securities firms, and insurers proceeded in 1999. In the interval this bill sat unfinished, the Glass-Steagall restrictions it would have repealed and the antitrust review it would have streamlined stayed in place — a temporary advantage for depositors and communities concerned about consolidation.

sides.party_line_note: In the House the vote split by party — 153 of 227 Republicans yes versus 61 of 205 Democrats yes, with the bill passing by one vote — while in the Senate the procedural votes were nearly unanimous and bipartisan, 93-0 and 88-11, with no party-line pattern in the opposition.

industries.note: The bill's core would let well-capitalized bank holding companies become financial holding companies combining banking, securities, and insurance, while limiting the Federal Reserve's ability to examine the new nonbank affiliates and easing antitrust review of bank mergers. The risks of affiliate trouble fall on insured banks and the deposit insurance funds that protect depositors.

Repealing Glass-Steagall opens bank deposit funding and bank customer bases to securities firms, and subjects bank securities activities to SEC functional regulation. Investors gain new one-stop competition but bear the risk of underwriting conflicts inside bank-affiliated firms.

Insurers gain access to bank distribution channels and preemption of some state affiliation limits, but banks entering insurance sales are required to buy existing licensed agents and are barred from underwriting most state-regulated products, protecting incumbent agents. State insurance regulation is preserved as the functional regulator.

industries.industry: Community banks and small financial institutions
industries.note: The bill streamlines antitrust review of bank mergers and repeals the bar on approving mergers that create monopolies, exposing small institutions to consolidation pressure from expanded giants; the bill orders a study of the impact on institutions with $100 million or less in assets.
